purpose: Evaluate whether structured training teaches Qwen3-VL-4B to recover the canonical observable maps and diagnose student errors in composed rigid transformations. The final model succeeds on map and diagnosis scoring, but its retained hint field has a known answer-disclosure failure.

inScope: Canonical observable RED-to-GREEN and RED-to-BLUE affine maps on coordinate-grid transformation diagrams, matching the Common Core 8.G standard.
Paired image-only and image+coordinates evaluation with modality-specific Qwen3-VL-4B adapters and one strict JSON diagnosis schema.
An eight-label diagnosis taxonomy, deterministic geometry scoring, and separate hint-safety auditing.

spov.claim: Structured training taught a 4B model the canonical map and diagnosis behavior that coordinate prompting alone did not provide. On paired 500-example cells, every untuned base arm had 0 exact correct-map and 0 exact two-map successes, while tuned image+coordinates reached 98.6% exact two-map accuracy on test.
spov.whySpiky: The evidence isolates learned task behavior from input convenience. Exact coordinates did not make the untuned model solve the canonical maps, but the same representation became useful after training on canonical net targets.
spov.argument: Four external benchmarks establish composition as a real model weakness. The project’s own paired evaluation then shows the base-to-tuned gain directly. The fair Opus comparison is mixed rather than a sweep: image-only map recovery is split, while the tuned model leads on the task-specific diagnosis labels; both coordinate models hit the geometry ceiling on n=50.
spov.bet: The falsifiable test was whether the base coordinate arm would recover canonical maps or the trained arm would fail to produce a large paired gain. The observed 0/500 base and 493/500 tuned test result supports the learning claim on this fixed evaluation.
spov.changeMind: A paired rerun that lets the base coordinate arm solve the maps, or that fails to reproduce the trained gain, would overturn the central claim. The current evidence does not establish broad frontier superiority, universal OOD generalization, or safe hint generation.

insights.title: Independent benchmarks isolate the composition gap
insights.body: Mind’s Eye reports 82% human versus 13.0-51.8% model accuracy on Mental Composition. TangramPuzzle reports 72.67% human versus 0-22.60% model full-composition success. DORI reports 86% human versus 8.6-49% model compound-rotation accuracy, and LEGO-Puzzles reports 93.6% human versus 54-59% model overall accuracy. These benchmarks motivate the target behavior, but they do not replace the project’s paired evaluation.
insights.drawsOn: Mind’s Eye, DORI, TangramPuzzle, LEGO-Puzzles, and question 1.2.

insights.title: Canonical map learning is the central result
insights.body: All four untuned base cells had 0/500 exact correct-map matches and 0/500 exact two-map matches, including coordinate input. The tuned image+coordinates arm reached 493/500 exact two-map matches and 498/500 direct labels on test, plus 497/500 exact two-map matches and 499/500 direct labels on the restricted OOD split.

insights.title: Coordinates help after training, not by themselves
insights.body: The separately trained image-only arm reached 192/500 exact two-map matches on test and 338/500 on restricted OOD. Image+coordinates reached 493/500 and 497/500. Because the untuned coordinate cells still had zero exact two-map successes, the comparison supports coordinates as a useful trained representation rather than a prompt-time solution. The two tuned modalities use different adapters, so this is an arm-level ablation.
insights.drawsOn: The paired base-to-tuned results and modality-specific training design.

insights.title: The fair Opus result is mixed
insights.body: On paired image-only n=150, tuned Qwen versus Opus scored 66 vs 71 correct maps, 59 vs 83 student maps, 53 vs 50 both maps, 126 vs 59 direct labels, and 126 vs 68 derived labels. No difference was detected for correct-map or both-map recovery; Opus was stronger on student-map recovery. On image+coordinates n=50, both models scored 50/50 on all geometry and derived-label metrics, while direct labels were 50/50 versus 40/50. The ceiling and task-specific taxonomy prevent a broad superiority claim.

insights.title: Independent checks support the map and diagnosis result
insights.body: All 4,000 saved base and tuned rows parse and preserve paired ID order. Local recomputation matched the saved aggregates, and offline rescoring reproduced all 20 requested tuned counts and rates with zero delta. The saved contamination audit reports zero exact training/evaluation geometry overlaps and zero training rows sourced from test or OOD, although the full training file was unavailable for a local fingerprint rerun.
insights.drawsOn: OVERNIGHT_REPORT.md and the frozen v6 result artifacts.

insights.title: Hint safety failed and must stay separate from map accuracy
insights.body: A blinded paired n=100 gpt-5.6-sol judge preferred tuned overall 100/0/0 after being told to respect deterministic correctness, but preferred base hints 75/25. It flagged answer or coordinate disclosure in 100/100 tuned hints versus 1/100 base hints. The deterministic audit found disclosure in 1,919/2,000 tuned hints and only 28/2,000 met the conservative safe/useful rule. The v6 prompt requested a short Socratic hint but omitted the legacy explicit no-coordinate prohibition, making this a specification and target-design failure rather than a direct violation of that exact prompt.

questions.title: Does AI actually fail at composed transformations? (the litmus-test check)

sources.title: Mind’s Eye: A Benchmark of Visual Abstraction, Transformation and Composition for Multimodal LLMs.

facts.text: Human baseline on Mental Composition (MC, chained transformations): 82%, almost identical to single-operation Mental Transformation (81%) and Paper Folding (80.1%). Humans show almost no composition penalty.
Models score 13.0-51.8% on MC, 10.1-35.6% on single transformation, 11.3-32.0% on folding, which is far below humans with wide variance.
“models particularly struggle with tasks requiring interpreting temporal sequences and tracking visual elements across transformations.”

sources.analysis: This is the most directly on-target paper found: it isolates composition as its own axis and shows models don’t just do worse than humans overall, they lose a specific, disproportionate amount of ground on the composed condition specifically.

sources.authors: Liu, Kuang, Li, Li, Yin, Cao, Sun, Shen, Zheng, Lin, Yu.
sources.title: TangramPuzzle: Evaluating MLLMs with Compositional Spatial Reasoning.
sources.institution: Tsinghua, Sun Yat-Sen, Tencent Youtu Lab, UIC.

facts.text: Outline Prediction (recognize the shape after transformations): up to 98.65% (Gemini3-Pro).
End-to-end full-composition success (generate the exact transformation sequence): Gemini3-Pro 22.60%, Claude-Sonnet-4.5 0.15%, GPT-5.2 0%, nearly all others 0-0.15%.
Human baseline on full composition: 72.67%.
“MLLMs tend to prioritize matching the target silhouette while neglecting geometric constraints.”

sources.analysis: Models go from near-perfect (98.65%) to near-zero (0-22.6%) purely by moving from “recognize the transformed shape” to “produce the composed transformation sequence,” while humans barely drop (72.67%, still far above any model). This is about as clean a “well-prompted base model can’t already do this reliably” result as the assignment’s litmus test could ask for.

sources.authors: Tasnim, Nichols, Yan, Ikechukwu, Zou, Ghadiyaram, Plummer.
sources.title: “Seeing Isn’t Orienting” (DORI benchmark).

facts.text: Human compound rotation accuracy: 86% coarse / 86% granular; only a 6-point penalty vs. single-axis rotation (92%/82%).
Model compound rotation: collapses to ~49% coarse, as low as 8.6% granular for closed-source models.
“models competent on general spatial benchmarks remain near-random on object-centric orientation tasks,” with “the largest drops on compound rotations.”

sources.analysis: A third independent lab, a third independent benchmark, the same qualitative shape: humans barely notice composition, models fall off a cliff. Three-for-three convergence across IIT Hyderabad/MSR, Tsinghua/Tencent, and Boston University is much stronger evidence than any single paper.

sources.authors: Tang, Gao, Zeng, Duan, Sun, Xing, Liu, Lyu, Chen.
sources.title: LEGO-Puzzles: How Good Are MLLMs at Multi-Step Spatial Reasoning?

facts.text: Human baseline: 93.6% overall; top models (GPT-4o, Gemini-2.0-Flash, Claude-3.5-Sonnet): 54-59%.
The “Ordering” task (sequence correct assembly steps) shows several models at near-zero accuracy.
Chain-of-thought prompting gives only “limited help,” with benefit “diminishing as task complexity increased beyond two steps.”

sources.analysis: Important negative result for mitigation strategy: if CoT prompting on a frontier model can’t fix this even at just two steps, that’s further confirmation prompting alone won’t clear the litmus test, reinforcing that this is a fine-tuning-shaped problem, not a prompting-shaped one.

subnodes.title: What does NOT count as evidence (explicitly ruled out)

sources.title: GeoEval (arXiv:2402.10104), GeoLaux (arXiv:2508.06226), and the Geometry3K/UniGeo/GeoQA/PGPS9K/MathVista cluster.

facts.text: These are the most-cited diagram geometry benchmarks, but on direct inspection they test static proof/calculation geometry (angles, lengths, congruence proofs, auxiliary-line construction). None isolate rotation/reflection/translation composition.

sources.analysis: A useful negative finding, not a gap in the search: the *mainstream* geometry-QA literature doesn’t test this behavior at all. The real evidence lives in the more tangential puzzle/spatial-cognition literature (tangrams, LEGO, origami, orientation benchmarks) above, not in “geometry problem solving” benchmarks despite the topical adjacency.

questions.title: Can a diagram be reliably converted to text first? (the pipeline’s first stage)

subnodes.title: Diagram parsing is a real, quantified bottleneck

sources.title: PGDP5K: A Diagram Parsing Dataset for Plane Geometry Problems.
sources.institution: Beijing Jiaotong University + Institute of Automation, CAS.

facts.text: State-of-the-art diagram parsing (PGDPNet) on PGDP5K achieves only 66.07% F1. Even a purpose-built, dedicated diagram parser mis-extracts roughly a third of diagram elements/relations.

sources.analysis: The single most load-bearing number for this project’s pipeline design: it directly quantifies the risk in stage 1 (diagram-to-text). No parser here was built for transformation-sequence diagrams specifically, so there’s no reason to expect better than ~66% F1 on this project’s diagram type without dedicated fine-tuning of that stage too.

sources.authors: Lu, Gan, Jiang, Qiu, Huang, Liang, Zhu.
sources.title: Inter-GPS: Interpretable Geometry Problem Solving with Formal Language and Symbolic Reasoning.
sources.institution: UCLA VCLA + Zhejiang University + Sun Yat-sen University.

facts.text: Parses diagram (Hough Transform + RetinaNet + MathPix OCR) and text into a shared formal logic language, then runs symbolic theorem-proving. 57.5% overall solving accuracy on their introduced Geometry3K dataset (3,002 problems). The diagram-parser-only accuracy ablation could not be independently verified.

sources.analysis: The foundational precedent for “parse the diagram into a formal/symbolic representation, then solve symbolically rather than end-to-end”. This is directly the architecture this project’s pipeline proposes, applied to a different geometry sub-domain.

sources.title: TALENT: Table VQA via Augmented Language-Enhanced Natural-text Transcription.
sources.institution: Johns Hopkins, Purdue, University at Albany.

facts.text: Pure OCR/markdown decomposition (73.6-75.5%) underperforms a richer “dual representation” (OCR spans + natural-language narration) decomposition (80.7-81.1%), which beats strong end-to-end VLMs (54.5-74.2%).
“Even with perfect OCR, an LLM reasoning over a rigid, non-prose format can still fail to grasp the full context.”

sources.analysis: The key qualifier on the whole pipeline idea: decomposition only helps if the intermediate text representation is *rich* (preserves spatial relationships, labeled correspondences, transformation parameters). A bare “here are two shapes” description would likely reproduce this paper’s failure mode.

sources.authors: Zhang, Cheng, Deng, Tian, Ma, Qin, Zhang, Zhu, Leng.
sources.title: “Diagram Formalization Enhanced Multi-Modal Geometry Problem Solver” (DFE-GPS).
sources.institution: Peking University, 201.AI, Shanghai Jiao Tong, Shanghai University.

facts.text: Adding a raw geometry diagram *decreases* accuracy for several MLLMs relative to text-only input (QwenVL: 19.90%→9.05%, a -10.85 point drop). Formalizing the diagram into a symbolic language before reasoning reverses this and improves further (+4-6 points over direct diagram+question input).

sources.analysis: The strongest direct support in the whole research pass, because it’s the only paper that runs on geometry diagrams specifically, on the same models: raw diagram hurts, symbolic diagram helps. Directly validates the “convert to text/symbolic form first” design choice for this project’s domain.

sources.title: Symbolic Grounding Reveals Representational Bottlenecks in Abstract Visual Reasoning.
sources.institution: Tallinn University of Technology + Kimova AI.

facts.text: On Bongard-LOGO-style abstract visual reasoning, end-to-end VLM on raw images: 50-51% (chance level). LLM reasoning over structured symbolic descriptions of the same scenes: up to 96.2%.
“poor performance in the visual setting stems primarily from representational limitations rather than an inability to reason over structured input.”

sources.analysis: The starkest decomposed-vs-end-to-end gap found (~45 points), though on a synthetic benchmark. It is directionally consistent with DFE-GPS and DePlot (chart QA: 29-point gain from decomposition), suggesting this is a general property of current VLMs, not a geometry-specific quirk.

questions.title: What do students actually get wrong when composing transformations? (the misconception taxonomy)

subnodes.title: The one verified, composition-specific misconception in the literature

sources.title: Student Proficiency with Transformational Geometry After a College Proof-Based Geometry Class.

facts.text: Of 17 preservice teachers asked whether a triangle-mapping isometry was unique, 7 justified an incorrect answer by asserting an isometry can only be “one move." It explicitly failing to recognize that a composition of transformations is itself a single transformation.
“These students wrote claims such as, ‘Yes because any other isometry would require more than one isometry.’”

sources.analysis: It’s a conceptual/proof-context error (composed-pair-vs-single-transformation conflation), not a computational one (wrong order, wrong center, wrong direction) like this project’s diagnoser will actually need to detect in computed-answer problems.

subnodes.title: The gap that matters most for this project

sources.authors: Fife, J. H., James, K., & Bauer, M.
sources.title: A Learning Progression for Geometric Transformations.

facts.text: Explicitly places “performs composition of simple transformations” at Level 3 and “understands associativity/commutativity of compositions” at Level 5 of a 5-level progression; but the report’s own dedicated “Common Misconceptions” section names **zero** composition-specific misconceptions, only single-transformation ones (e.g., “a rotated square is no longer a square,” “circles can’t be translated because they have no corner ‘handles’”).

sources.analysis: A document explicitly built to catalog transformation misconceptions, from a top psychometric research org, simply doesn’t have a composition-specific entry. This is a genuine, informative absence: the field has not consolidated a named, measured misconception taxonomy for composed transformations. This project’s misconception label set must be constructed and empirically validated from scratch (informed by the plausible-but-unmeasured error types the AI-failure literature keeps gesturing at: order-dependence assumptions, not updating the reference frame/center for the second transformation) rather than imported from prior research.

experts.name: Pan Lu
experts.institution: UCLA Center for Vision, Cognition, Learning, and Autonomy (VCLA)
experts.views: Geometry problem solving benefits from parsing diagrams into a shared formal/symbolic language before applying symbolic theorem-proving, rather than reasoning end-to-end on pixels (Inter-GPS); later work (MathVista) catalogs how far multimodal models still are from reliable visual math reasoning.
experts.whyFollow: Author of Inter-GPS and the Geometry3K dataset, which is the foundational precedent for this project’s “diagram → text/symbolic → solve” pipeline architecture, applied to a different geometry sub-domain (proofs/calculation rather than composed transformations).

experts.name: Bryan A. Plummer / Deepti Ghadiyaram
experts.views: Current VLMs remain near-random on object-centric orientation reasoning even when they perform well on general spatial benchmarks; the gap is largest specifically on compound/composed rotations, not single-axis ones.
experts.whyFollow: Co-authors of DORI, one of three independent benchmarks (alongside Mind’s Eye and TangramPuzzle) that converge on the exact “composition collapses, single-step doesn’t” pattern this project’s litmus test relies on.

experts.name: Aditya Kanade / Tanuja Ganu (Microsoft Research Bengaluru) + Rohit Sinha (IIT Hyderabad)
experts.views: Multimodal LLMs disproportionately fail on tasks requiring tracking visual elements across a sequence of transformations (Mental Composition), compared to single-operation transformation or even paper-folding (forward-tracking) tasks.
experts.whyFollow: Authors of Mind’s Eye, the single most directly on-target benchmark found. It isolates “composition” as its own measured axis with a human baseline, which is exactly the comparison this project’s evaluation suite needs to replicate.

experts.name: Cheng-Lin Liu (Institute of Automation, CAS)
experts.institution: NLPR, Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences
experts.views: Plane-geometry diagram parsing should be treated as its own measurable sub-task (not folded into end-to-end solving accuracy), because even dedicated parsers leave substantial extraction error.
experts.whyFollow: Senior author associated with PGDP5K/PGDPNet, the source of this project’s most load-bearing risk number (66.07% F1 ceiling on dedicated diagram parsing).

experts.name: Tamara (Terry) Fukawa-Connelly
experts.views: Preservice teachers frequently hold a “one move” conception of isometries that prevents recognizing a composition of transformations as itself a single well-defined transformation.
experts.whyFollow: Co-author of the only verified, quantified, composition-specific misconception finding in the math-education literature located during this research pass; a starting point (not a complete taxonomy) for this project’s misconception label set.

experts.name: Educational Testing Service (Fife, James, Bauer)
experts.views: Geometric transformation understanding progresses through 5 measurable levels, with composition-of-transformations appearing at Level 3 and commutativity/associativity understanding at Level 5. Their own misconceptions catalog, built explicitly to be comprehensive, contains no composition-specific entries.
experts.whyFollow: The clearest documented signal that this project cannot source its misconception taxonomy from existing literature and must construct + validate one empirically.
